title: Shakun Batra: Bollywood Romances Fail Gen Z Because They Are 'Far From Reality'
excerpt: The Lust Stories 3 director told HT City that trend-chasing meetings can't manufacture connection — only authenticity can.
body:
• Filmmaker Shakun Batra told HT City that Bollywood romances fail to connect with Gen Z because the love stories they show remain “far from reality” — built on a fantasy of instant, perfect love that real life never delivers.
  • Batra argued that directors cannot reverse-engineer what young audiences want: “I need to portray what I am feeling and what I need to express,” he said, rejecting trend-chasing meetings where “ye chal raha hai” (this is working) dictates creative choices.
  • The director, whose recent segment in Netflix's Lust Stories 3 explores a complex romance between two people in their 20s, said authenticity — not formula — is what earns a younger audience's trust.

Shakun Batra has a diagnosis for why Bollywood's love stories leave Gen Z cold: the romance on screen is still a fantasy, and young audiences can tell.

“You meet this person who is your soulmate, and then life is amazing, but it never is,” the filmmaker told HT City, explaining why the genre keeps missing its mark with younger viewers. According to Batra, Bollywood's portrayal of romance remains far from real life — a gap that international streaming shows, with their messier and more grounded relationships, have exploited to win loyal young Indian followings.

Make what you feel, not what's trending

Batra's larger argument is about how films get made in the first place. Directors, he said, cannot put themselves inside somebody else's head and calculate what that person needs to watch. “I've been in many of those meetings where they're like, ‘Ye chal raha hai (this is working).' But mere se wo nahin ho raha hai (but I cannot do it), and that's why I've had enough breaks in my career,” he said.

“I need to portray what I am feeling and what I need to express and hope that I've done a job of simplifying it enough that somebody else can also receive it.”

— Shakun Batra, to HT City

Working any other way, he said, is “a work-for-hire kind of thing, where you feel that I need to make this person feel good” — and he cannot work that way. If a filmmaker puts their most authentic self out and does the job right, he argued, audiences will come around: “if not today, in a year or two, they will understand and accept it.”

Practice, not theory

Batra is speaking from recent practice. His segment in Netflix's Lust Stories 3 traces a complicated romance between two people in their 20s, and co-star Radhikka Madan has said the portrayal felt so real that people called her with their own relationship stories — the kind of recognition formula romances rarely earn.

The anthology, which also features segments by Kiran Rao, Vikramaditya Motwane and Vishal Bhardwaj, has kept Batra in the middle of the industry's ongoing argument about desire, intimacy and morality on screen — an argument where he and Motwane have both pushed back against what Motwane calls the “gatekeepers” behind the backlash to bold films.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora audience — raised on both Bollywood's grand romances and Hollywood's dating realism — Batra's critique lands in familiar territory. The generation gap he describes plays out in NRI households too, where parents' DDLJ-era ideals of love meet children's dating-app reality. His prescription, make it true rather than make it sell, is the bridge.

What's next

Whether the industry listens is another matter. Bollywood's romance machine runs on opening-weekend math, and authenticity is a harder pitch than a hit song. But with streaming audiences rewarding honesty over spectacle, Batra's bet is that the filmmakers who refuse to chase trends will outlast the ones who do.
